extracted.intended_audience: academic economists, policy researchers, and graduate students studying mortgage markets, shadow banking, and fintech
extracted.subtask_description: An academic empirical and quantitative-modeling analysis of how regulatory burdens and technological improvements affected shadow bank and fintech market shares and lending in the residential mortgage market (2008–2015). Combines reduced-form regressions, event-study and IV strategies, bootstrap inference, and a calibrated structural model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome variables (change in market share and lending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two outcome variables: the change in shadow bank market share between 2008 and 2015, and the growth in shadow bank lending between 2008 and 2015 measured as a share of all 2008 lending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining changes in market share isolates shadow bank growth relative to banks; examining changes in lending levels tests whether shadow bank market share rises because banks reduce lending or because shadow banks actively expand lending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of regulatory burden (four measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: County-level regulation measures include changes in capital ratios, MSR (mortgage servicing rights) percentage of tier 1 capital, lawsuit exposure, and OTS (Office of Thrift Supervision) origination share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To facilitate comparison, each measure is standardized by dividing by the cross-sectional standard deviation so coefficients are interpretable as percent changes in market share or lending volume for a one standard deviation change in the regulation variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression specification and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline regressions take the form Δ(outcome) = α + β Regulation_r + δ X + BΓ + ε, where Regulation_r is one of the standardized regulation measures and X includes county characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control variables include demographics and traditional bank share in 2008. Regressions are run with year and county fixed effects and with county-level control coefficients allowed to vary by year (in event study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted least squares by 2008 originations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because counties differ greatly in lending activity, regressions are run as weighted least squares weighted by 2008 originations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weights account for heterogeneous county size so estimates reflect lending-activity–weighted associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of coefficients (std-dev interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coefficients on standardized regulation variables can be interpreted as percent changes in market share or lending volume associated with a one standard deviation change in the regulation variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization enables comparison across different regulation measures (e.g., capital ratio changes vs. MSR exposure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-study / difference-in-differences design
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel event study comparing high-regulation counties to others over time: (outcome)_{c,t} = sum_j γ_j HighReg_c × 1{year=j} + county FE + year FE + controls varying by year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High_reg is defined as counties in the top quintile of MSR% of tier 1 capital or OTS origination share. Timing of policy events (MSR rule finalization in 2013, OTS shutdown in 2011) is used to assess whether market-share jumps align with event dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental-variable strategy for capital ratio increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrument increases in capital ratios between 2008 and 2015 with capital ratio decreases between 2006 and 2008.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis: counties whose banks experienced the largest capital decreases during the crisis rebuilt capital the most after 2008; use first-stage and second-stage (2SLS) to isolate causal effect of capital rebuilding on shadow bank growth. Report reduced-form and second-stage results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest-rate pricing regressions and R2 as measure of information use
rubrics_metrics.description: Regress observed interest rates on borrower, loan, and property characteristics to measure how much variation in interest rates is explained by observable (hard) information. Compute within R2 after differencing out fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate separately for fintech and non-fintech lenders and year-by-year. Lower R2 for fintech interpreted as fintech using less hard information (and possibly other big-data inputs) in pricing. Test significance of R2 differences using bootstrap method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bootstrap test for significance of R2 differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Bootstrap by sampling with replacement from originated loans, split into fintech and non-fintech samples, rerun interest-rate regressions for 100 resamples, and compute the distribution of R2 differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test statistic is the t-value of the R2 difference across fintech and non-fintech samples; present distribution (e.g., Fig. 7) and infer significance (differences significant beyond 1% level reported).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of ex-post performance (default and prepayment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether lenders' interest rates are predictive of ex-post loan performance (default and prepayment) to evaluate whether pricing reflects superior information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find little difference regarding default (limited GSE exposure) but large differences for prepayment; interpret cautiously because borrower selection into lenders (e.g., refinancing-prone borrowers choosing fintech) may bias results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience and price-discrimination test (High FICO interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether fintech's pricing premium varies by borrower willingness-to-pay using a High FICO dummy (top 10% FICO) and interaction with fintech indicator in interest-rate regressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coefficient on fintech captures baseline premium for ordinary borrowers; interaction captures additional premium for High FICO borrowers. Results: higher-FICO fintech borrowers pay an additional premium, consistent with convenience value and willingness-to-pay heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple regression specifications and nonlinear controls for robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate multiple specifications with different fixed effects, more controls, and polynomials of controls to ensure patterns (e.g., R2 differences) are not driven by omitted nonlinearities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in saturated specifications, reported patterns (R2 differences) persist, supporting robustness of inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and supplementary materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Use binned scatter plots and online appendices (e.g., Online Appendix A.9, A.5, A.2, A.7) to show data variation, bootstrap distributions, subgroup results, and classification procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual evidence supports robustness and helps illustrate relationships across values of regulatory exposure and other measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative structural model framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple equilibrium model with three lender types (banks, non-fintech shadow banks, fintech shadow banks) differing in regulatory burden, convenience quality, and marginal cost; demand u = −α r + q + ε; regulatory constraints scale bank market shares by γ_s; supply includes marginal cost ρ_i and fixed entry cost c_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model determines pricing, entry, markups, and market shares endogenously; equilibrium defined by borrower utility maximization, lender profit-maximizing pricing, and free entry (zero profit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration targets and normalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Calibrate model annually (2008 onward) to zip-year mean data: number of firms of each type, market shares, pricing of each type, and market size. Measure funding costs relative to the ten-year government yield and normalize bank quality (q_bank) = 0 and γ_s = 1 in 2008.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain α by inverting banks' first-order condition; invert first-order conditions of shadow lenders to get marginal costs; calibrate non-fintech and fintech quality from market shares and rates (Eqs. 33–34); invert relative market shares to infer regulatory burden (Eq. 35); use zero-profit condition to back out fixed entry costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition experiments using the calibrated model
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfactual exercises: (1) fix regulatory burden and fintech quality at 2008 levels; (2) allow regulatory burden to evolve but hold fintech quality fixed; (3) hold regulatory burden fixed but allow fintech quality to evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use calibrated model to attribute observed shadow-bank growth to regulatory tightening vs. technology: e.g., regulatory changes explain ~12% shadow-bank growth; technology explains ~8.3% fintech share gain and ~90% of fintech gains; combine to compare against observed growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of calibrated results and policy linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret increases in calibrated regulatory burden after 2011 as corresponding to Dodd-Frank implementation, Basel III MSR treatment changes, CFPB establishment, and increased mortgage lawsuit activity; interpret fintech quality improvements and funding-cost dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss mechanism: regulatory changes operate primarily via extensive-margin constraints reducing banks' ability to lend; fintech funding costs rise as entrants scale, and fixed costs increase implying rising entry barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification robustness for fintech vs non-fintech
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification protocol: use multiple independent research assistants and authors to classify lenders; where RAs disagree, take a conservative approach and classify as non-fintech; verify historical classification using archived websites from the Internet Archive Wayback Machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that classifications in 2016 map back to 2008–2010 (major lenders); ensure no large traditional banks would have been classified as fintech in earlier years. Document classification process and report sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks section
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a number of robustness checks concerning lender classification, sample selection, and other concerns that might impact inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly report alternate specifications and checks (e.g., restricting sample to 2010 onward, different classification rules) and note whether results change materially.
